title: Sangria Hangover: Why the Pitcher Hits So Hard and How to Avoid It
excerpt: Why sangria hangovers feel so bad: hidden alcohol in the pitcher, added brandy, red wine congeners, and sugar. How much is really in a pitcher, and how to enjoy it without the morning after.
metaDescription: Why sangria gives such bad hangovers: how much alcohol is really in a pitcher, the role of wine and sugar, and how to drink it without paying tomorrow.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a sangria hangover is usually not about some special ingredient. It's about how much alcohol you drank without noticing. Sangria is wine (often with brandy or orange liqueur added), sweetened so the alcohol barely registers, and served from a pitcher that keeps refilling your glass. By the time the pitcher is empty, many people have had the alcohol of half a bottle of wine or more, often in the sun and often without much food. Red wine's congeners may add a little extra punch, but the pitcher effect is the main story.

**The quick rules:** Count every glass of sangria as at least one drink, and as more if the recipe has brandy or liqueur. Pour smaller glasses and don't top up a half-full glass. Eat a real meal with it, drink water between glasses, and lean toward lighter recipes with more sparkling water and fruit. If you're already hungover, rehydrate, eat something gentle, and rest. There is no good evidence that any pill or trick cures a hangover fast.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most sangria hangovers are unpleasant but pass within a day. **Get medical help right away (call 911 in the US) if** someone is confused, very hard to wake, has slow or irregular breathing, seizures, blue-tinged lips, or can't stop vomiting. These can be signs of alcohol poisoning, which is an emergency. **See a doctor soon if** you can't keep fluids down for many hours, you're seeing blood in vomit, you have severe stomach pain, your symptoms last well beyond a day, or you get hives, wheezing, or swelling after drinking wine (which can point to a sensitivity rather than a hangover). If you notice shaking, sweating, or anxiety that only eases when you drink again, that's worth raising with a doctor too. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Sangria Hangovers Feel So Bad: The Pitcher Effect

Sangria has a reputation as a light, summery drink. In reality it's one of the easiest drinks to overdo, and the reasons have more to do with how it's served than what's in it.

### 1. You can't taste the alcohol

Fruit, juice, sugar, and soda hide the sharp taste of alcohol. That's the whole appeal, and it's also the trap. When a drink tastes like punch, your brain doesn't send the usual "slow down" signals that come from the taste of straight wine or spirits. People tend to sip sweet drinks faster and treat them more like a soft drink than a glass of wine.

### 2. The pitcher keeps refilling your glass

With a bottle of beer or a single cocktail, you know when you've finished one. With a pitcher, someone tops up your glass when it's half empty, and then again. You never finish a glass, so you never count one. This is the same reason people underestimate how much they drink at parties where wine is being poured for them.

### 3. Glasses are often big and full of ice and fruit

Sangria is usually served in large wine glasses or tumblers. A big pour can easily hold more than a standard 5-ounce serving of wine. Ice melts and fruit soaks up liquid, so it's hard to judge how much you're actually drinking.

### 4. Many recipes add spirits

Classic Spanish-style sangria is red wine with fruit, a little sugar, and often a splash of brandy. Many modern recipes add brandy, rum, triple sec, or flavored liqueur on top of the wine. That can push a glass of sangria up to the strength of straight wine or higher, even though it tastes weaker.

### 5. It's a daytime, outdoor, social drink

Sangria shows up at brunches, barbecues, beach days, and long summer dinners. Afternoon sun and heat make you sweat, you may not be drinking much water, and a long social session means you're drinking over many hours. All of that adds up to more alcohol and less hydration than a normal evening.

Put together, these factors explain most sangria hangovers. The drink isn't uniquely toxic. It's uniquely good at helping you drink more than you meant to.

## How Much Alcohol Is Actually in a Pitcher of Sangria?

This is the part most people never work out, so here's a worked example. In the US, a **standard drink** is about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly 5 ounces of wine at 12% alcohol, 12 ounces of regular beer, or 1.5 ounces of 40% spirits.

A typical homemade pitcher might look like this:

| Ingredient | Amount | Approximate standard drinks |
|---|---|---|
| Red wine (about 12.5% alcohol) | One 750 ml bottle | About 5 |
| Brandy (40% alcohol) | Half a cup (about 4 oz) | About 2.5 to 3 |
| Orange liqueur, such as triple sec | A quarter cup (about 2 oz) | About 1 |
| Orange juice and sparkling water | About 2 cups | 0 |
| **Whole pitcher** | **Roughly 6 to 7 glasses** | **Roughly 8 to 9** |

These are rough numbers, and every recipe is different. Liqueurs range widely in strength, and some people use far more brandy than this. But the takeaway holds up: **a single pitcher can easily contain the alcohol of eight or nine standard drinks.** If two people share one pitcher over dinner, each has had about four drinks. If a second pitcher arrives, you're well into the range that gives most people a real hangover.

A recipe made with only wine, fruit, and juice or soda is lighter, roughly five standard drinks across the pitcher. That's the same as a full bottle of wine, just spread across more glasses.

### Bottled, canned, and restaurant sangria

Store-bought sangria varies a lot. Some bottled sangrias are lower in alcohol than regular wine, and some canned "sangria spritz" style drinks are lighter still. Others are fortified and closer to full-strength wine. The only reliable guide is the ABV on the label. Restaurant sangria is the hardest to judge because you can't see the recipe, and pitchers and glass sizes vary from place to place. When in doubt, assume each glass is at least one full drink.

For a sense of how a bottle of wine breaks down into servings, see our guide on [how many drinks are in a bottle of wine](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-in-a-bottle-of-wine).

## The Wine Factor: Congeners, Histamine, and Sulfites

Once you've accounted for the amount of alcohol, the wine itself can still play a supporting role. Most sangria is made with red wine, and red wine has a few features that may make hangovers worse for some people.

### Congeners

Congeners are the extra compounds produced during fermentation and aging, beyond the alcohol itself. They include things like methanol, other alcohols, and various flavor compounds. Darker drinks such as red wine, whiskey, and brandy generally contain more congeners than clear drinks like vodka or white wine.

Research has linked higher-congener drinks to somewhat worse hangovers. A well-known study by Rohsenow and colleagues, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010, found that people rated their hangovers as worse after drinking bourbon than after the same amount of vodka. The difference was real but modest. The amount of alcohol was still the bigger factor.

Sangria often combines two higher-congener drinks: red wine and brandy. That doesn't make it poisonous, but it's one more reason a sangria morning can feel rough.

### Histamine and tannins

Red wine contains more histamine than white wine, and it also contains tannins, the compounds that give it a dry, puckering feel. Some people seem sensitive to these and get headaches, flushing, or a stuffy nose from red wine even in small amounts. Alcohol may also interfere with how your body breaks down histamine. The research here is mixed, and it's far from settled why some people get red wine headaches and others don't. If red wine reliably gives you a headache after one glass, our guide to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) and our look at [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) go into more detail.

### Sulfites

Sulfites get blamed for a lot, but the evidence that they cause headaches in most people is weak. Sulfites are a real issue for a small number of people, especially some with asthma, who can have breathing problems or allergy-like reactions. Many common foods, including dried fruit, contain more sulfites than wine does. For most people, sulfites aren't the reason sangria hurts. Our article on [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) covers this in depth.

## Does the Sugar in Sangria Cause Hangovers?

This is one of the most common questions, and the honest answer is that **there is no good evidence that sugar itself causes hangovers.** The idea that "sugary drinks give you the worst hangovers" is popular, but the research doesn't clearly support it.

What sugar does do is indirect:

- **It hides the alcohol.** Sweet drinks are easier to drink quickly and in large amounts. That's the biggest way sugar contributes to a sangria hangover.
- **It can add to a blood sugar dip.** Alcohol can interfere with how your liver releases sugar into the blood, especially if you haven't eaten. A big hit of sugar followed by hours of drinking can leave you shaky, tired, and very hungry the next morning. That's worse on an empty stomach.
- **It makes sangria calorie-heavy.** A few glasses can add up to a lot of calories, which doesn't cause a hangover but is worth knowing.

### What about diet mixers?

Some people switch to diet soda or sugar-free mixers to make sangria lighter. That cuts calories, but it doesn't make the drink safer. A study by Marczinski and Stamates, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2013, found that mixing alcohol with diet soda led to higher breath alcohol levels than mixing it with regular soda. The likely reason is that sugar slows how fast the stomach empties into the intestine, where alcohol is absorbed. So "sugar-free sangria" isn't a hangover hack. It may get the alcohol into your blood faster.

### And the bubbles?

Recipes that use sparkling water, soda, or sparkling wine add carbonation. There's some evidence that carbonated alcoholic drinks are absorbed faster than flat ones, although results vary between people. Faster absorption means a quicker rise in blood alcohol, which can make it harder to judge how drunk you are. Sparkling water is still a good way to stretch a pitcher and lower the alcohol per glass, so the trade-off usually favors adding it.

## Red Sangria vs White Sangria vs Rosé Sangria

People often ask whether switching the wine changes the hangover. A little, maybe.

| Type | What changes | Hangover angle |
|---|---|---|
| **Red sangria** | Red wine base, often with brandy | Highest in congeners, histamine, and tannins. Most likely to bother people sensitive to red wine. |
| **White sangria** | White wine, often with peach, citrus, or elderflower liqueur | Generally fewer congeners and less histamine. Often sweeter, with added liqueur. |
| **Rosé sangria** | Rosé base, usually with berries and soda | In between. Often lighter in style, but just as easy to over-pour. |
| **Sparkling sangria** | Topped with cava, prosecco, or soda | Bubbles may speed absorption a little. Sparkling wine adds alcohol, soda doesn't. |

If you get headaches from red wine specifically, a white or rosé sangria may suit you better. But the color of the wine is a small factor compared with how many glasses you drink and whether spirits were added. A pitcher of white sangria with peach schnapps can leave you just as wrecked as a red one. For more on how wine styles compare, see our full [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide).

## How to Enjoy Sangria Without Paying for It Tomorrow

You don't have to give up sangria. These steps target the real causes, which are the hidden amount of alcohol, the pace, and the conditions you drink in.

### Make it lighter

- **Skip or cut the spirits.** A recipe with wine, fruit, and juice is noticeably lighter than one with brandy and liqueur. If you like the flavor of brandy, use a small splash rather than half a cup.
- **Stretch it with sparkling water.** Use more sparkling water or club soda and less wine. You keep the fizz and fruit and lower the alcohol in every glass.
- **Use more fruit and ice.** A glass full of fruit holds less liquid.
- **Choose a lighter wine.** Wines vary from around 11% to 15% alcohol. A lower-alcohol wine makes a lighter sangria.

### Control the pour

- **Use smaller glasses.** A regular wine glass filled halfway is closer to a real serving than a big tumbler filled to the top.
- **Finish your glass before refilling.** Don't let anyone top you up. It's the easiest way to keep count.
- **Keep track.** Count each glass as at least one drink, more if the recipe has spirits. If you're sharing pitchers, divide the pitcher by the people drinking from it.

### Set up your body

- **Eat a real meal.** Food in your stomach slows alcohol absorption. Sangria pairs naturally with tapas, grilled food, and paella, so lean into that. Our guide to [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.
- **Drink water between glasses.** One glass of water for each glass of sangria slows your pace and helps with hydration, especially in the heat.
- **Get out of the sun now and then.** Long afternoons in the heat add sweat loss on top of alcohol's effect on your kidneys.
- **Set a stopping point before you start.** Decide on a number of glasses, or a time to switch to non-alcoholic drinks. It's much easier to stick to a plan made while sober.

### Try a mocktail round

A non-alcoholic sangria made with grape juice, a splash of tea or pomegranate juice, citrus, and sparkling water looks and tastes close to the real thing. Alternating rounds is a simple way to stay in the party without doubling your alcohol. If you're mixing your own drinks, our guide to the [best mixers to avoid a hangover](/never-hungover/best-mixers-to-avoid-hangover) has more ideas.

## How to Treat a Sangria Hangover

There's no fast cure for a hangover. Time is the only thing that fully fixes it, and most hangovers fade within about 24 hours. What you can do is ease the symptoms while your body recovers.

### Rehydrate

Alcohol makes you pass more urine, and a day in the sun adds sweat on top of that. Start with water, then add something with electrolytes if you feel drained or have been sick. Sip slowly if your stomach is unsettled. Our guide to [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) walks through what works.

### Eat something gentle

If you had a lot of sweet sangria and not much food, low blood sugar may be part of why you feel shaky and weak. Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, rice, or soup are easy on the stomach and help steady your energy. You don't need a lot of sugar to fix this. A normal, balanced meal works better than candy.

### Handle the headache carefully

- **Ibuprofen or naproxen** can help a hangover headache for many people. Take it with food and water, stick to the label dose, and skip it if you have stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or take blood thinners. Alcohol already irritates the stomach, so don't take these on an empty stomach.
- **Avoid acetaminophen (Tylenol) after heavy drinking.** It's processed by the liver, which is already working on the alcohol. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the risk.
- **Don't take painkillers "just in case" before bed.** Wait until you wake up and actually need one.

### Rest and skip the "hair of the dog"

Sleep after drinking is usually poor quality, so a nap or an early night helps. Having another drink in the morning only delays the hangover. It doesn't cure it.

### Know what's normal and what isn't

A headache, tiredness, thirst, mild nausea, and a low mood are typical. Repeated vomiting, confusion, chest pain, a racing heart that won't settle, or symptoms that go on well past a day are not typical, and they're a reason to call a doctor or get urgent care. See the box at the top of this page for the emergency signs.

## Why Sangria Might Hit Some People Harder Than Others

Two people can share a pitcher and wake up feeling completely different. Some reasons:

- **Body size and sex.** Smaller people, and women on average, reach higher blood alcohol levels from the same amount of drink.
- **Food.** Drinking on an empty stomach means faster absorption and a higher peak.
- **Sensitivity to red wine.** Some people react to red wine with headaches and flushing even at low amounts, for reasons that aren't fully understood.
- **Sleep.** A late night with little sleep makes any hangover worse.
- **Genetics.** Some people break down alcohol's by-products more slowly, especially many people of East Asian descent who flush when they drink. They often feel worse after drinking.
- **Medications.** Some medicines interact with alcohol and can make you feel much worse, or are unsafe to mix. If you take regular medication, check with a pharmacist about alcohol.

## A Note on DHM and Supplements

You'll see many supplements marketed as hangover helpers. The most studied is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Animal and lab studies suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol and its by-products, but the human evidence is limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers, and it doesn't change how much alcohol is in your pitcher. The steps above, especially lighter recipes and smaller pours, will make a bigger difference.

If you're curious to try it alongside those habits, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands honestly. If you take medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Sangria hangovers are mostly about **hidden alcohol**: sweet taste, big glasses, endless refills, and recipes with brandy or liqueur.
- A single pitcher can hold **roughly five to nine standard drinks**, depending on the recipe.
- Red wine's congeners and histamine may add to the misery for some people, but they're a smaller factor than the amount you drink.
- There is no good evidence that sugar itself causes hangovers. It mainly makes sangria easier to drink fast. Diet mixers don't make it safer.
- Make it lighter, pour smaller, finish each glass before a refill, eat a meal, and drink water between glasses.
- For a hangover, rehydrate, eat something gentle, rest, and use ibuprofen with food if it's safe for you. Avoid Tylenol after heavy drinking.
- Get help right away for signs of alcohol poisoning, such as confusion, being hard to wake, slow breathing, or repeated vomiting.

For how this drink compares with the rest, see our [ranking of alcohol from least to most hangover](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) and our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does sangria give me such a bad hangover?**

Mostly because it's easy to drink more alcohol than you realize. Sangria is wine, often with brandy or orange liqueur added, and the fruit and sugar hide the taste of alcohol. It's served from a pitcher, so glasses get topped up and nobody counts. A single pitcher can hold the alcohol of a full bottle of wine or more. Red wine's congeners, the extra by-products of fermentation, may add to the misery, but the amount you drank matters most.

**Is sangria stronger than wine?**

It depends on the recipe. Sangria made with only wine, fruit, and juice or soda is a bit weaker than straight wine per glass, because the mixers dilute it. Sangria with brandy, rum, or triple sec added can be about as strong as wine, or stronger. Bottled and canned sangrias vary widely, so check the ABV on the label. The real issue is that sangria glasses tend to be big and refilled often.

**How many drinks are in a pitcher of sangria?**

A typical homemade pitcher made with one 750 ml bottle of wine has about five standard drinks from the wine alone. Add half a cup of brandy and a splash of orange liqueur and the total rises to roughly eight or nine standard drinks. Restaurant pitchers vary, so if you're splitting one between two people, assume you've each had several drinks.

**Does the sugar in sangria make a hangover worse?**

There is no good evidence that sugar itself causes hangovers. The bigger problem is that sweetness masks the alcohol, so you drink faster and more. Sugary drinks on an empty stomach can also leave you feeling shaky and hungry later as your blood sugar drops. If you love sangria, eat a real meal with it and keep the pitcher count in mind.

**Is white sangria or red sangria better for a hangover?**

White sangria may be slightly gentler for some people because white wine generally has fewer congeners and less histamine and tannin than red wine. But white sangria often gets extra sugar and liqueur, and it's just as easy to over-pour. The amount of alcohol you drink matters far more than the color of the wine.

**What's the best thing to do for a sangria hangover?**

There's no fast cure. Drink water or an electrolyte drink, eat something gentle like toast, eggs, or soup, and rest. Ibuprofen with food can help a headache if you can take it safely, but avoid acetaminophen (Tylenol) if you drank heavily. Most hangovers ease within 24 hours. Get medical help if you can't keep fluids down, you're confused, or symptoms are severe or unusual.

**How can I drink sangria without getting a hangover?**

Pour smaller glasses, count each glass as at least one drink, and skip refills until your glass is empty. Make or order versions without added brandy or liqueur, use more sparkling water and fruit, eat a full meal, and drink a glass of water between glasses. Nothing guarantees you won't get a hangover except drinking less, but these steps lower the odds.
